source_text: DE patientia locuturus, fratres dilectissimi, et utilitates ejus et commoda praedicaturus, unde potius incipiam quam quod nunc quoque ad audientiam vestram patientiam video esse necessariam, ut nec hoc ipsum quod auditis et discitis, sine patientia facere possitis. Tunc enim demum sermo et ratio salutaris efficaciter discitur, si patienter quod dicitur audiatur. Nec invenio, fratres dilectissimi, inter caeteras coelestis disciplinae vias quibus ad consequenda divinitus praemia spei ac fidei nostrae secta dirigitur, quid magis sit vel utilius ad vitam vel majus ad gloriam, quam ut qui praeceptis dominicis obsequio timoris ac devotionis innitimur, patientiam maxime tota observatione tueamur. Hanc se sectari philosophi quoque profitentur. Sed tam illic patientia falsa est, quam et falsa sapientia est. Unde enim vel sapiens esse vel patiens possit qui nec sapientiam nec patientiam Dei novit? quando ipse de his qui sibi sapere in mundo videntur moneat et dicat: Perdam sapientiam sapientium, et prudentiam prudentium reprobabo. Item beatus apostolus Paulus, plenus Spiritu sancto et vocandis formandisque Gentibus missus, contestetur et instruat dicens: Videte ne quis vos depraedetur per philosophiam et inanem fallaciam, secundum traditionem hominum, secundum elementa mundi, et non secundum Christum, quia in ipso habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis. Et alio loco: Nemo se, inquit, decipiat. Si quis se putat sapientem esse in vobis, mundo huic stultus fiat, ut fiat sapiens. Sapientia enim mundi hujus stultitia est apud Deum. Scriptum est enim: Reprehendam sapientes in astutia ipsorum. Et iterum: Cognovit Dominus cogitationes sapientium, quia sunt stultae. Quare, si sapientia illic vera non est, esse non potest et vera patientia. Nam si sapiens ille est qui est humilis et mitis, philosophos autem nec humiles videmus esse nec mites, sed sibi multum placentes, et hoc ipso quod sibi placeant Deo displicentes, apparet illic veram non esse patientiam ubi sit insolens affectatae libertatis audacia et exerti ac seminudi pectoris inverecunda jactantia. Nos autem, fratres dilectissimi, qui philosophi non verbis sed factis sumus, nec vestitu sapientiam, sed veritate praeferimus, qui virtutum conscientiam magis quam jactantiam novimus, qui non loquimur magna sed vivimus, quasi servi et cultores Dei, patientiam quam magisteriis coelestibus discimus obsequiis spiritalibus praebeamus. Est enim nobis cum Deo virtus ista communis. Inde patientia incipit, inde claritas ejus et dignitas caput sumit. Origo et magnitudo patientiae Deo auctore procedit. Diligenda res homini quae Deo chara est: bonum quod amat majestas divina commendat. Si dominus nobis et pater Deus est, sectemur patientiam domini pariter et patris: quia et servos oportet esse obsequentes, et filios non decet esse degeneres. Qualis vero in Deo et quanta patientia, quod, in contumeliam suae majestatis et honoris instituta ab hominibus profana templa et terrena figmenta et sacra sacrilega patientissime sustinens, super bonos et malos aequaliter facit diem nasci et lumen solis oboriri, et cum imbribus terras rigat, nemo a beneficiis ejus excluditur quominus justis similiter et injustis indiscretas pluvias largiatur! Videmus inseparabili aequalitate patientiae nocentibus et innoxiis, religiosis et impiis, gratias agentibus et ingratis, Dei nutu tempora obsequi, elementa famulari, spirare ventos, fontes fluere, grandescere copias messium, fructus maturescere vinearum, exuberare pomis arbusta, nemora frondescere, prata florere. Et cum crebris immo continuis exacerbetur offensis Deus, indignationem suam temperat, et praestitutum semel retributionis diem patienter exspectat. Cumque habeat in potestate vindictam, mavult diu tenere patientiam, sustinens scilicet clementer et differens, ut, si fieri potest, multum malitia protracta aliquando mutetur, et homo in errorum et scelerum contagione volutatus vel sero ad Deum convertatur, ipso monente et dicente: Nolo mortem morientis, quantum ut revertatur et vivat. Et iterum: Revertimini ad me, dicit Dominus. Et iterum: Revertimini ad Dominum Deum vestrum, quoniam misericors et pius et patiens et multae miserationis, et qui sententiam flectat adversus malitias irrogatas. Quod item beatus apostolus Paulus commemorans et peccatorem ad poenitentiam revocans, proponit et dicit: An numquid opulentiam bonitatis ejus et sustinentiam et patientiam contemnis, ignorans quoniam patientia et bonitas Dei ad poenitentiam te adducit? Tu autem, secundum duritiam tuam et cor impoenitens, thesaurizas tibi iram in die irae et revelationis justi judicii Dei, qui reddet unicuique secundum opera sua. Justum judicium Dei dixit esse, quia serum est, quia diu multumque differtur, ut homini ad vitam longa Dei patientia consulatur. Tunc repraesentatur poena impio et peccatori, quando jam non potest poenitentia prodesse peccati.
pass_a_gloss: About to speak on patience, dearest brothers, and to proclaim its advantages and benefits, whence rather shall I begin than that now also to your hearing patience I see is necessary, so that not even this thing which you hear and learn, without patience you are able to do. For then at last a sermon and a saving discourse is effectively learned, if what is said is patiently heard. Nor do I find, dearest brothers, among other heavenly discipline ways by which to attain divinely the rewards of our hope and faith, what is more or more useful to life or greater to glory, than that we who lean on the Lord's precepts with obedience of fear and devotion, should especially guard patience with all observation. This also philosophers profess to follow. But just as false is patience there, as also false is wisdom there. For whence can someone be wise or patient who knows neither the wisdom nor the patience of God? Since He Himself warns and says about those who seem to be wise in the world: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject. Also blessed apostle Paul, full of the Holy Spirit and sent to call and form the Gentiles, testifies and instructs saying: See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ, because in Him dwells all the fullness of divinity. And in another place: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks he is wise, let him become foolish in this world, so that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: I will reprove the wise in their cunning. And again: The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are foolish. Wherefore, if wisdom is not true there, neither can true patience be. For if he is wise who is humble and mild, but we see that philosophers are neither humble nor mild, but pleasing to themselves, and by this very fact that they please themselves, they displease God, it appears that true patience is not there where there is the audacity of affected freedom and the shameless boasting of an exerted and semi-nude heart. But we, dearest brothers, who are philosophers not in words but in deeds, and who prefer wisdom not in clothing but in truth, who know the conscience of virtues rather than boasting, who do not speak great things but live them, as servants and worshippers of God, we offer patience which we learn from heavenly teachings through spiritual obedience. For this virtue is common to us with God. From there patience begins, from there its clarity and dignity take their start. The origin and greatness of patience proceed from God as author. The thing to be loved by man which is dear to God: the good which divine majesty loves, it commends. If the Lord is our master and Father God, let us follow the patience of the Lord and Father alike: because it is fitting for servants to be obedient, and for sons not to be unworthy. But what kind and how great is the patience in God, that, in contempt of His majesty and honor, profane temples and earthly figments and sacrilegious rites instituted by men, He most patiently endures, and over good and evil alike makes the day rise and the sun's light shine, and with rains He waters the earth, no one is excluded from His benefits so that He gives indiscriminate rains to the just and the unjust alike! We see with inseparable equality the patience towards the harmful and the innocent, the religious and the impious, those giving thanks and the ungrateful, God's nod obeying the times, the elements serving, the winds breathing, the fountains flowing, the crops of harvests growing, the fruits of vineyards ripening, the trees abounding with fruit, the groves leafing, the meadows flowering. And although God is provoked by frequent, indeed continuous, offenses, He tempers His indignation, and patiently awaits the predetermined day of retribution. And although He has vengeance in His power, He prefers to hold patience for a long time, sustaining and deferring, so that, if it can be, the wickedness, having been prolonged, may sometime be changed, and man, having been rolled in the contagion of errors and crimes, may turn to God, even if late, God Himself warning and saying: I do not wish the death of the dying, but that he may turn and live. And again: Turn to me, says the Lord. And again: Turn to the Lord your God, for He is merciful and pious and patient and of great mercy, and who turns judgment against inflicted wickedness. Which also blessed apostle Paul, commemorating and recalling the sinner to penitence, proposes and says: Or do you despise the riches of His goodness and tolerance and patience, ignoring that the patience and goodness of God lead you to penitence? But you, according to your hardness and impenitent heart, treasure up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works. He said that the just judgment of God is, because it is late, because it is deferred for a long time, so that man may be consulted for a long life by God's patience. Then punishment is represented to the impious and the sinner, when already penitence can no longer benefit the sin.

pass_b_english: I am about to speak on patience, dearest brothers, and to proclaim its advantages and benefits. Where better to begin than with the very patience that I see is necessary for your hearing right now, so that you may not even be able to do this thing that you hear and learn without patience? For only then is a sermon and a saving discourse effectively learned, if what is said is patiently heard. Nor do I find, dearest brothers, among the other ways of heavenly discipline by which our sect is directed toward the attainment of divinely bestowed rewards of hope and faith, anything more useful for life or greater for glory than that we, who lean on the Lord's precepts with the obedience of fear and devotion, should especially guard patience with all observance. Philosophers also profess to follow this virtue. But the patience there is just as false as the wisdom there is false. For how can anyone be wise or patient who knows neither the wisdom nor the patience of God? Since He Himself warns and says concerning those who seem to be wise in the world: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject" (1 Corinthians 1:19; Job 5:13). Also the blessed apostle Paul, full of the Holy Spirit and sent to call and form the Gentiles, testifies and instructs, saying: "See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ, for in Him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:8–9). And in another place: "Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, 'He catches the wise in their craftiness,' and again, 'The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile'" (1 Corinthians 3:18–20; Psalm 94:11). Therefore, if wisdom is not true there, true patience cannot exist there either. For if the wise man is he who is humble and gentle, we see that philosophers are neither humble nor gentle, but are pleased with themselves, and by this very fact that they please themselves they displease God. It is apparent that true patience is not there where there is the audacity of an affected freedom and the shameless boasting of an exerted and semi-nude breast. But we, dearest brothers, who are philosophers not in words but in deeds, and who prefer wisdom not in clothing but in truth, who know the conscience of virtues rather than boasting, who do not speak great things but live them, as servants and worshippers of God, let us offer the patience that we learn from heavenly teachings through spiritual obediences. For this virtue is common to us with God. From there patience begins; from there its clarity and dignity take their start. The origin and greatness of patience proceed from God as author. A thing is to be loved by man which is dear to God; the good that divine majesty loves, it commends. If the Lord is our master and God our Father, let us follow the patience of the Lord and of the Father alike: because it is fitting for servants to be obedient, and for sons not to be degenerate. But what kind and how great is the patience in God? He most patiently endures profane temples and earthly figments and sacrilegious rites instituted by men in contempt of His majesty and honor. Over the good and the evil alike He makes the day rise and the light of the sun shine, and with rains He waters the earth; no one is excluded from His benefits, so that He bestows indiscriminate rains on the just and on the unjust alike (Matthew 5:45)! We see, with an inseparable equality of patience, the harmful and the innocent, the religious and the impious, those giving thanks and the ungrateful, all obeying God's nod as the times serve, the elements serving, the winds blowing, the fountains flowing, the crops of harvests growing, the fruits of vineyards ripening, the trees abounding with fruit, the groves leafing, the meadows flowering. And although God is provoked by frequent, indeed continuous, offenses, He tempers His indignation and patiently awaits the predetermined day of retribution. And although He has vengeance in His power, He prefers to hold patience for a long time, sustaining and deferring, so that, if it can be, prolonged wickedness may sometime be changed, and man, having been rolled in the contagion of errors and crimes, may turn to God, even if late, God Himself warning and saying: "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 18:23; 33:11). And again: "Return to me, says the Lord." And again: "Return to the Lord your God, for He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love, and relents over disaster" (Joel 2:13). The blessed apostle Paul also commemorates this, recalling the sinner to repentance, and proposes and says: "Or do you presume on the riches of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God's righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works" (Romans 2:4–6). He said that the judgment of God is just because it is late, because it is deferred for a long time, so that by the long patience of God man may be provided for a long life. Then punishment is represented to the impious and the sinner when repentance can no longer benefit the sin.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text, including the nuances of the philosophical critique and the theological arguments regarding God's patience. Scripture citations in Pass B are correctly identified and added as required (e.g., Colossians 2:8-9, Matthew 5:45, Ezekiel 18:23, Romans 2:4-6) and match the Latin allusions.
